Its range is moderately low, less bright than the classical guitar, yet with the deep flavour of the guqin. Because the body is pear-shaped, the cavity is relatively small, which gives a moderate volume that still carries well, particularly suited to the accompanying role in a folk band. Plucked with a goose quill the timbre is soft and pliable; next to the clear brightness of the modern lute the cobza sounds fuller and more reserved. Its chordophone nature means every pluck brings a subtle overtone, creating a plain, elegant atmosphere. The cobza is an instrument of the multi-string lute family in the folk music of Romania, Moldova and contemporary Hungary, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-6. It has a pear-shaped wooden body, a short neck, a pegbox bent back and a ribbed back, usually with double or triple courses; Romanian versions mostly use metal strings, and nylon strings are also found in modern Hungary. It is played with a folded goose quill or a plectrum, traditionally providing rhythm and harmony in folk music, and it can also be played solo or in an ensemble; the bridge has a wide string spacing, which suits elaborate melodies. It is not the same as the Ukrainian kobza.
羅馬尼亞科布扎魯特琴的起源可能為波斯巴爾巴特琴或土耳其烏德琴的本地改編，15世紀: The Romanian cobza may be a local adaptation of the Persian barbat or the Turkish oud, brought in by wandering Roma musicians in the fifteenth century. Use of related instruments in Hungary goes back at least to the sixteenth century, and they may have arrived with the Magyar tribes in the ninth or tenth. The modern Romanian cobza came into use in Hungary with the dance-house movement at the end of the twentieth century. Bukovina also used it in wartime, and after the northern part was incorporated into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic it was replaced by the mandolin and the four-string domra. Its development also shows a metal-string tradition, more nylon strings in Hungary, and a fretted version in the Republic of Moldova.
